design_detail: Single-author narrative review (Maastricht University) of next-day (residual) effects of benzodiazepine and benzodiazepine-like sleeping pills. Part 1 summarizes epidemiological studies of traffic crashes, falls and hip fractures (case-control, case-crossover and cohort studies, Tables II to IV). Part 2 compares drugs and doses using three chosen sources: an expert survey from 1989 to 1990 (45 experts; a technical report, Table VI), a 1998 meta-analysis of 812 experimental studies of 248 medicines (Berghaus; Table VII) and eleven studies with a standardized on-road highway driving test calibrated against blood alcohol (Figures 1 to 3). Ends with the author's categorization of residual effects by drug, dose and time after a bedtime dose (Table VIII) and advice to prescribers.
can_establish: As summarized second-hand, which benzodiazepine sleeping pills and doses impaired next-morning on-road driving in the standardized test (and by how much compared with blood alcohol levels), how expert ratings and an older meta-analysis ranked them, and what case-control and cohort studies up to about 2002 reported on crashes, falls and hip fractures in people prescribed them.
cannot_establish: Pooled or appraised effect sizes (no systematic search, no pooling, no formal appraisal); whether the accident associations are causal (observational studies with confounding by indication, as the author notes); effects in people with insomnia who take the pills for months or years; or anything published after about 2003.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Cited epidemiology: for example a Saskatchewan cohort of 225 796 people prescribed a benzodiazepine and 97 862 controls (Neutel), a UK case-crossover study of 19 386 drivers in a first traffic accident (Barbone et al., 1998), and studies of adults over 65 (Hemmelgarn et al., 1997; Leveille et al., 1994; Ray et al., 1992) (Table II, p. 306). Driving-test studies were in healthy volunteers or women with insomnia who had used hypnotics before (p. 316).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated. The author chose to rely mainly on the expert survey, the Berghaus meta-analysis and the standardized driving test because studies differ too much to compare (p. 299).
sample.demographics: Not applicable. The meta-analysis drew mostly on studies of 12 or fewer participants, usually healthy young men (p. 315).
sample.selection_effects: Driving-test evidence comes from one research tradition (Dutch on-road test laboratories, largely the author's group); experimental studies are mostly single doses in healthy volunteers; epidemiological studies can show risks only for commonly prescribed drugs (p. 314).

exposure.measurement: As in the cited studies: prescription records or interviews in the epidemiological studies; administered doses in the experimental studies.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, as summarized: bedtime doses of flunitrazepam 1 and 2 mg, flurazepam 15 and 30 mg, loprazolam 1 and 2 mg, lormetazepam 1 and 2 mg, nitrazepam 5 and 10 mg, temazepam 20 mg, triazolam 0.125, 0.25 and 0.5 mg, zaleplon 10 and 20 mg, zolpidem 10 and 20 mg and zopiclone 7.5 mg (p. 299); driving tests 10 to 11 hours after a bedtime dose and, in six studies, again 16 to 17 hours after; some after two nights or a week of nightly use (p. 316, p. 322).
exposure.polysubstance: Epidemiological studies: use of several drugs together is described as a consistent risk factor for falls and fractures (pp. 311, 313); alcohol use generally not separable in the prescription-record studies.

comparison.controls: Placebo in the experimental studies; non-exposed periods or people in the epidemiological studies.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The author notes that insomnia itself, the reason for prescribing and prescribers' choices (for example safer drugs for frailer patients) can confound the epidemiological comparisons (p. 314).

outcomes.instruments: Epidemiology: injurious crashes, police-reported accidents, falls and hip or femur fractures. Experiments: expert ratings of impairment (0 none to 3 severe) by time after dosing; percentage of performance measures significantly worse than placebo (Berghaus); standard deviation of lateral position (SDLP, weaving) in a one-hour, 100-km on-road highway drive (p. 316).
outcomes.validity_norms: The on-road test was calibrated in 24 social drinkers: blood alcohol concentrations of 0.5, 0.8 and 1.0 g/L raised SDLP by 2.4, 4.2 and 5.1 cm on average; test-retest reliability r = 0.7 to 0.9 (p. 316).
outcomes.operationalization: Residual impairment expressed as the alcohol level that would produce the same weaving.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported for the cited studies.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates. Second-hand figures: on-road driving 10 to 11 hours after a bedtime dose was impaired more than at a blood alcohol concentration of 1.0 g/L after flurazepam 30 mg and loprazolam 2 mg; at levels equivalent to 0.5 to 0.8 g/L after nitrazepam 10 mg, flunitrazepam 2 mg, zopiclone 7.5 mg, oxazepam 50 mg, lormetazepam 2 mg capsules and flurazepam 15 mg; not significantly after lormetazepam 1 mg capsules, temazepam 20 mg soft capsules or nitrazepam 5 mg (p. 316). Traffic crashes: odds ratios after a new hypnotic prescription 6.5 (95% CI 1.9 to 22.5) in weeks 1 to 2 and 3.9 (1.9 to 8.3) in weeks 1 to 4, falling to 1.4 in the second month (Neutel); 1.2 (0.8 to 1.7) for hypnotics and 2.2 (1.5 to 3.1) for anxiolytic benzodiazepines in a case-crossover study (Barbone et al.) (Table II, p. 306).
analysis.covariates: As in the cited studies; not summarized.
analysis.selective_reporting: Driving-test results are shown only for the studies with comparable procedures (Figures 1 to 3); others are described in text.
analysis.power: The author notes that most experimental studies were too small to detect minor or moderate impairment and most epidemiological studies too small for rarely prescribed drugs (pp. 314-315).

interpretation_gap.results_show: As summarized: several benzodiazepine sleeping pills, especially long-acting ones and higher doses, impaired next-morning driving in on-road tests by as much as or more than alcohol at common legal limits, while some lower doses of shorter-acting ones did not detectably impair it; use of sleeping pills was associated with more crashes, mostly early after starting, and with falls and hip fractures in older people, with inconsistent results across studies.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions (pp. 297-298, 323-324) present the summary table as a quick reference that lets clinicians choose drugs and doses unlikely to produce residual effects; this categorization mixes measured results with expert opinion from 1989 to 1990 and the author's judgment, and the categories 'unlikely' rest largely on non-significant results in small studies.

timeline.event: Johnson and Chernik review 52 placebo-controlled studies: dose is the main determinant of next-day impairment (as summarized, p. 300; not in the library's references).
Johnson et al.: morning caffeine reduced next-day sleepiness after triazolam or flurazepam in a small laboratory trial (not cited by this review)
Fornaro et al.: network meta-analysis of next-morning driving after sleep medicines, including several of the same on-road studies

replication.where_it_stands: Its driving-test summary is broadly consistent with the later network meta-analysis (flurazepam and triazolam impairing; temazepam and low-dose lormetazepam not detectably so), but the two share primary studies and are not independent.

funding.funder: Not reported: the article states that the author provided no information on sources of funding (Acknowledgements, p. 324).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: no information on conflicts of interest directly relevant to the content (p. 324).
funding.affiliations_note: Experimental Psychopharmacology Unit, Maastricht University; many of the on-road driving studies cited are from the author's group and collaborators.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review with a reported search and appraisal of on-road and simulator driving trials of each benzodiazepine sleeping pill, plus prescription-linked crash studies that separate sleeping pills from daytime anxiolytics and model time since starting, with results for people with insomnia who take the pills nightly for months.

domains.note: No search or inclusion criteria; the author chose three sources for the drug comparison and does not say how the epidemiological studies were found.
No formal appraisal, but the limits of the epidemiological designs (confounding by indication, exposure misclassification, low power) and of small experimental studies are discussed (pp. 313-315).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The on-road driving evidence comes largely from the author's own research group and collaborators.
Table VIII mixes measured effects, expert opinion and the author's judgment without marking which is which; prescribing advice follows directly.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how long and how much next-day impairment lasts
domains.note: Null and positive findings are both reported, but evidence in people with insomnia who take the pills long term, where tolerance could reduce residual effects, is under-represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The review is careful about epidemiological limitations, but its selection is unsystematic and its central comparison relies on the author's own driving-test tradition, an unpublished expert survey from 1989 to 1990 and a German-language meta-analysis report. Cite it for the on-road driving results it summarizes (with page and figure), for the alcohol calibration of the driving test, and as a pointer to the epidemiological studies; claims resting only on it stay at draft and say their figures are second-hand.

key_findings.finding: The on-road highway driving test was calibrated against alcohol: blood alcohol concentrations of 0.5, 0.8 and 1.0 g/L increased weaving (SDLP) by 2.4, 4.2 and 5.1 cm on average, in 24 social drinkers; test-retest reliability r = 0.7 to 0.9.
key_findings.locator: 4.3 Standardised Highway Driving Test, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: In driving tests 10 to 11 hours after a bedtime dose, flurazepam (higher dose) and loprazolam (higher dose) impaired driving more than a blood alcohol concentration of 1.0 g/L; nitrazepam, flunitrazepam and lormetazepam at their higher doses, flurazepam at the lower dose, oxazepam and zopiclone impaired it to a degree equal to 0.5 to 0.8 g/L; lormetazepam (lower dose, capsules), temazepam (soft capsules) and nitrazepam (lower dose) had no significant residual effect. Doses on the card's exposure field.
key_findings.locator: 4.3, right column, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figures 2 and 3 (pp. 320-322; bar charts, values not extracted)
key_findings.note: Second-hand summary of studies from the author's research tradition; the sentence on flurazepam and loprazolam is internally contradictory (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: In the afternoon test (16 to 17 hours after the dose), impairment declined rapidly for the short- and intermediate-acting drugs but remained or even increased for the long-acting flunitrazepam and nitrazepam.

In shift workers sleeping by day, triazolam (higher dose) produced driving impairment equivalent to a blood alcohol concentration over 1.0 g/L after the first treatment and about 0.8 g/L after the fifth, with driving 7.5 to 8.5 hours after the dose.

With nightly use, impairment after flurazepam (higher dose) increased slightly over 7 nights and persisted after the first night without the drug, suggesting accumulation; impairment after nitrazepam (higher dose) did not diminish from the second to the seventh night; lormetazepam soft capsules (higher dose) peaked after 4 nights and then declined; temazepam soft capsules and lormetazepam (lower dose) showed no residual effects throughout a week.

In expert ratings (0 none to 3 severe) for 8 to 12 hours after a bedtime dose, flurazepam (higher dose) was rated 3.0, nitrazepam (higher dose) 2.8, flunitrazepam 2.8 and 2.6 at the two doses on the exposure field, triazolam (highest dose) 2.7, temazepam soft capsules 1.0 and lormetazepam (lower dose) 0.6.

Traffic crashes: after a new prescription for a hypnotic (triazolam or flurazepam), odds ratios for an injurious crash were 6.5 (95% CI 1.9 to 22.5) in the first two weeks, 3.9 (1.9 to 8.3) in the first four weeks and 1.4 in the second month (Saskatchewan cohort, Neutel); in a UK case-crossover study the odds ratio was 1.2 (0.8 to 1.7) for hypnotics, 2.2 (1.5 to 3.1) for anxiolytic benzodiazepines and 4.0 for zopiclone (Barbone et al.).
key_findings.locator: 3.1 Traffic Accidents, 2nd to 4th paragraphs; Table II
key_findings.note: Second-hand; the zopiclone odds ratio is given in the text without an interval.

key_findings.finding: In adults aged 65 or over, crash risk was not increased for benzodiazepines with half-lives of 24 hours or less (odds ratio 1.0, 95% CI 0.8 to 1.3) and was 1.5 (1.0 to 2.0) for longer-acting ones in the first week (Hemmelgarn et al.); another study found no increase for hypnotics (0.9, 0.4 to 2.0; Leveille et al.).
key_findings.locator: Table II, rows Hemmelgarn et al. and Leveille et al.; 3.1, 5th paragraph (p. 307)

key_findings.finding: Falls and fractures in older people: a meta-analysis of 40 studies gave pooled odds ratios of 1.54 for sedatives and hypnotics and 1.48 for benzodiazepines; risk was highest in the first weeks of use (for example adjusted rate ratio 3.0 in week 1, 2.2 in weeks 2 to 4 and 1.3 after; odds ratio 3.6, 2.3 and 1.4 over the first two months) and rose with dose and with the number of drugs taken together.
The author advises that patients be told that not feeling sleepy or dizzy does not mean their performance is normal.

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence on flurazepam and loprazolam says their impairment was worse than at a blood alcohol concentration of 1.0 g/L in the morning or afternoon and also equivalent to 0.8 g/L in the afternoon, which cannot both be true.
reporting_issues.consequence: The afternoon size of their effect is unclear; the figures (bar charts without numbers) cannot resolve it.

reporting_issues.issue: The criterion used in the Berghaus meta-analysis is described as the effect of a blood alcohol concentration of 0.03 g/L, an implausibly low level (perhaps 0.3 g/L or 0.03%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The threshold for clinically relevant impairment in Table VII cannot be confirmed from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract names 11 hypnotics including midazolam, the list of drugs and doses in the introduction omits midazolam, and the tables add brotizolam and three anxiolytics.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the drugs covered differ by section.

reporting_issues.issue: The categorization in Table VIII, including a 4 to 8 hour column, is presented as a summary of results without saying how measured data, expert ratings and judgment were combined.
reporting_issues.consequence: Its categories should be cited as the author's judgment, not as findings.
